# PocketOne

> PocketOne is a community fork of PocketBase (one Go binary: database, auth, files, realtime, admin UI) with extensions for point-in-time recovery, backups, mail, many instances on one server, deploys, tokens and OAuth, MCP, and PocketPages server-rendered sites.

PocketOne takes the same commands and flags as PocketBase, plus its own; core PocketBase topics live at https://pocketbase.io/docs. Agent Skills for PocketOne and PocketPages: https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/tree/main/agent (Claude Code: `/plugin marketplace add pockethost/pocketone`).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/overview

# What is PocketOne?

PocketOne is a community fork of [PocketBase](https://pocketbase.io). It tracks upstream PocketBase and keeps its own
changes to the core small: only the hooks that let extensions extend and override PocketBase. Every feature lives in an
extension.

It's maintained by [PocketHost](https://pockethost.io), which runs it in production. PocketOne is not affiliated with
or endorsed by the PocketBase project.

## What it adds

Run `pocketone` the way you run `pocketbase`. These are the differences you'll notice.

### Point-in-time restore, on by default

Your database is replicated with Litestream, so you can restore it to any moment from **Settings → Backups** or with
`pocketone pitr restore`. Turn it off with `--pitr=false`.

### Mail you can see in dev mode

In dev mode (`serve --dev`), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send through the system's `sendmail`. The mail is
caught and shown at `http://127.0.0.1:8025`.

### Server-rendered pages

Put `.ejs` and Markdown files in a `pb_pages` folder and they're served as pages, with no build step. This site is
one. `pocketone pages create myapp` starts a new site from a starter kit. Full docs are under
[Pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages/overview).

### A config file

Settings can live in `pocketone.yaml`, with secrets in a `.env` file beside it that your JS hooks never see. Without
the file, PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. `pocketone config` lists every section, and
`pocketone config check` checks a file. The [config reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference) lists every section.

### Commands for working with remote apps

- `pocketone login`, `remote` and `link`: save logins to your apps.
- `pocketone deploy`, `dev`, `pull` and `logs`: ship `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public` to an app and
  watch it.
- `pocketone upgrade`: move to the latest release, keeping the old executable.
- `pocketone remote …`: every operation of every contract an app offers is a command, such as
  `pocketone remote restore to --at -2h`. The same operations are REST endpoints and MCP tools.
  [Remote administration](https://pocketone.dev/docs/remote) explains it, and the [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli) lists every command.

### Agents and API tokens

- An MCP endpoint at `/mcp` lets agents such as Claude manage your app and call its tools.
- Long-lived API tokens (`pbt_…`) with scopes, for scripts and integrations.
- Your app can act as an OAuth provider; `pocketone login` and MCP sign-in use it.

### Extensions that fit together

PocketOne's extensions meet through contracts: named, versioned promises like `restore/v1` that any extension can
keep. The dashboard, the `pocketone` command, agents and your `pb_hooks` call the contract, so you can swap the
extension behind it without changing anything else. [How PocketOne fits together](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together) explains it.

### Everything else

Automatic TLS certificates, bulk mail to your own users, scheduled VACUUM, signed S3 download redirects, and more. See
[all extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions).

## What stays the same

The admin dashboard, collections, rules, the REST and realtime APIs, JS hooks and migrations all work as in PocketBase.
For those, the [PocketBase docs](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketbase) are the reference.

## How it's built

- **A small core.** PocketBase's own code changes only to add hooks. Each change is marked in the source, reviewed by
  someone who didn't write it, and kept minimal so upstream releases merge cleanly. You can review the complete core
  changes [here](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone#changes-we-made-to-pocketbase).
- **Everything else is an extension.** Extensions live in `ext/` in the repo. Each is its own Go module, with a README and a
  small example.
- **Off until you use it.** The extensions in the `pocketone` binary add no work to an app that doesn't use them.
- **One app or hundreds.** An extension written against the extension contract works the same on a single app and on every
  instance under a multi-instance host.

## Open to contributions

PocketOne is open to everyone. Ask questions and share ideas in
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/discussions), report bugs in
[Issues](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/issues), and send extensions as pull requests. Start with
[Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension).

## Where to next

- [Install PocketOne](https://pocketone.dev/docs/installation)
- [Browse the extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions)


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/installation

# Installation

PocketOne is one executable, `pocketone`. It is built on PocketBase v0.41 and takes the same commands and flags, plus its own.

## Homebrew (macOS and Linux)

```bash
brew install pockethost/tap/pocketone
```

The formula lives in [pockethost/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/pockethost/homebrew-tap).

## Download a release

Download the zip for your platform from
[Releases](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/releases), unzip it, and put `pocketone` somewhere on your `PATH`.

## Build from source

With [Go](https://go.dev) installed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone.git
cd pocketone/examples/pocketone
go build -o pocketone .
```

## Run it

Create your first superuser before the first serve:

```bash
pocketone superuser upsert <email> <password>
pocketone serve
```

Opening `http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/` to create it also works, as in PocketBase.

To start a site with server-rendered pages:

```bash
pocketone pages create myapp
cd myapp
pocketone serve --dev --dir ./pb_data
```

In dev mode (`serve --dev`), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send mail through the system's `sendmail`. PocketOne
catches the mail and shows it at `http://127.0.0.1:8025`.

## Upgrade

```bash
pocketone upgrade
```

This replaces the executable with the latest release. The old one is kept beside it as `pocketone-<version>`, never
deleted, so you can go back.

## Moving from PocketBase

PocketOne reads the same `pb_data`, `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations` and `pb_public` folders. Point it at your existing data
directory with `--dir`, as you would with `pocketbase`. Back up `pb_data` first.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together

# Contracts: how PocketOne fits together

PocketOne is PocketBase plus extensions. What keeps those extensions from turning into a pile of plugins that know
too much about each other is how they meet: through **contracts**.

## The idea

A contract is a promise with a name and a version. `restore/v1` promises one thing: *put this app's data back as it
was at a moment*. It says what you can ask and what you get back. It says nothing about how.

An extension that keeps the promise **provides** the contract. Everything else talks to the contract, never to the
extension behind it: the dashboard, the `pocketone` command, an AI agent over MCP, your `pb_hooks`, and other
extensions.

That's the whole rule: **every API an extension offers is a contract.** Extensions have no private routes and never
import each other.

## An example: restore/v1

Every PocketOne app can restore its data to a moment. Who does the work depends on the app:

| Provider | How close it gets |
|---|---|
| [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr) | Any second in the last three days, from continuous history. |
| [Backups](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/backups), the default | The latest backup made at or before the moment. It steps aside when PITR is on. |
| A multisite host | It could restore an instance from the host's own disk snapshots. |

Asking looks the same whoever answers:

```bash
pocketone remote restore to --at -2h                                   # the command line
curl -X POST https://app.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore \
  -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -d '{"at": "2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}'      # HTTP
```

An agent asked to "restore my app to yesterday at 3pm" calls the same operation as an MCP tool. Settings → Backups
shows the contract's own "Restore to a moment" screen. The answer always says which point the data came from: exactly
3pm with PITR, or the 2:00 backup without it.

If something better than PITR comes along tomorrow, it provides `restore/v1`, and nothing that restores apps has to
change.

## Why it matters

- **Swap anything.** Any extension that provides a contract can stand in for another. One line in `pocketone.yaml`
  chooses when several could.
- **Build on anything.** Extensions depend on contracts, not on each other: Deploy requires `remote/v1`, not "the
  Remotes extension". Replace Remotes and Deploy keeps working.
- **One surface, promised.** If a client can call it, it's in a contract: named, versioned, documented and checked.
  Every extension route lives under `/api/_c/<contract id>/`; only paths a standard fixes stay at the root
  (`/.well-known/*`, `/mcp`).
- **Written once, reachable everywhere.** A contract's interface is the source for everything around it. Each
  operation is at once an HTTP endpoint, a `pocketone remote` command, an MCP tool, a hook in Go and in `pb_hooks`,
  and a typed client call. Every one of those paths passes the same checks: superusers only unless the operation is
  public, the token's scopes, and the action hooks.
- **Nothing hidden.** Each app prints who provides what when it starts; `pocketone remote whoami` lists the contracts
  an app offers; the [catalogue](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) lists every contract with the extensions that provide it, require it and
  work with it.

## What one interface gives you

Write the interface, run `go generate`, and a contract like `restore/v1` gets all of this:

| Surface | `restore/v1` |
|---|---|
| HTTP API | `GET /api/_c/restore/v1`, `POST /api/_c/restore/v1/restore` |
| Command line | `pocketone remote restore points`, `pocketone remote restore to --at -2h` |
| MCP tools | `restore_points`, `restore_restore_to` |
| Hooks | `restorev1.OnRestoreTo(app, ...)` in Go, `onRestoreRestoreTo(...)` in `pb_hooks` |
| Client | `restorev1.NewClient(url, token, nil).RestoreTo(...)` |
| Dashboard | "Restore to a moment" on Settings → Backups, shown for any provider |

## Who provides what

When an app starts, PocketOne settles every contract and says what it decided:

```
standard: restore/v1 ← pitr (default backups stepped aside)
standard: mail.fallback/v1 ← mailtrap
standard: deploy/v1 ← deploy (default)
```

- **Defaults.** A standard extension often provides a contract as the default: it steps aside as soon as anything
  else provides it.
- **Choices.** When two extensions provide a contract that takes one, the app won't start until `pocketone.yaml`
  picks one:

  ```yaml
  providers:
    restore/v1: pitr
  ```

- **Chains.** Some contracts take several providers in order. Mail with SMTP off goes through `mail.fallback/v1`'s
  chain: the dev inbox in dev mode, then a host's relay.
- **Your own JS.** An app's `pb_hooks` can provide contracts too, in `onContracts((e) => e.provide(...))`.
- **The host.** On a multisite host, some contracts are answered by the host for its instances. An instance running a
  stock PocketBase image in Docker has no PocketOne extensions inside it, but the host still answers `remote/v1` for
  it, so `pocketone remote logs` works there too. The host's own parts are contracts as well: what runs instances
  (`runtime/v1`, Pocker or Docker), what admits requests (`gate/v1`), its TLS (`tls/v1`).

## Versions

A contract's id carries its major version only: `restore/v1`. Within `v1` the promise doesn't change. Changing it
means a `restore/v2` beside `v1`, so whatever relies on `v1` keeps working. A new optional ability is usually a new,
small contract rather than a change to an old one.

## Where contracts live, and who owns them

Every contract, from the standard set or the community, lives in one place: `ext/contracts/<id path>/vN/`
(`mail.fallback/v1` is `ext/contracts/mail/fallback/v1/`). Extensions live in `ext/<name>/`. Keeping contracts
together means one namespace, so two authors can't publish different `rehash/v1`s, and it means one place to look
for what you can build on.

Each contract has a README like an extension's, with its owners and a one-line promise at the top. Its list of the
extensions that provide it, require it and work with it is generated from the code, so it's never out of date.

Whoever first creates a contract owns it. An extension author who needs a contract that doesn't exist yet writes it
first, and then owns both the contract and the extension that provides it. Changes to a contract are reviewed
carefully, because every provider and every caller relies on the promise. Name a contract for what it does
(`restore/v1`), not for the extension that happens to provide it first.

## Words

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Contract** | A named, versioned promise: a Go interface plus the API, commands, tools and hooks generated from it. |
| **Provide** | An extension keeps the promise for an app. |
| **Require** | An extension can't work without the contract; without a provider it's turned off, and the startup lines say why. |
| **Works with** | An extension uses the contract when something provides it. |
| **Default** | A provider that steps aside when any other extension provides the contract. |
| **Host-provided** | A multisite host answers the contract for its instances. |

## Next

- [Contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts): what each one promises, and who provides, requires and works with it.
- [Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension): declare, provide and use contracts in your extension.
- [Add a contract](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts#add-a-contract): the folder, the README and the generated code.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/remote

# Remote administration

Everything an extension lets you do to an app, you can do from afar, three ways:

- the `pocketone` command, against any app you've signed in to;
- the REST API, from a script or another service;
- MCP, from an agent such as Claude.

Nobody writes these by hand. Each extension API is a [contract](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together): a Go interface with one method per
operation. PocketOne generates the command, the endpoint and the tool from that interface. Install an extension, or
use a host that provides a contract, and its commands show up in the `pocketone` you already have. There's no other
tool to install.

## From your terminal

Sign in to an app once, then run its commands:

```bash
pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default
pocketone login prod
pocketone remote whoami        # who you are there, your token's scopes, and the contracts the app offers
pocketone remote restore points
pocketone remote restore to --at -2h
```

`remote restore to` calls [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) on the app. On an app with
[PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), you get the data as it was two hours ago, to the second. On an app with
[Backups](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/backups) only, you get the latest backup before that. The command is the same either way.

How a command is named and read:

- **Name:** `remote`, the contract's name, then the operation. restore/v1's `restore_to` is `remote restore to`,
  mail.suppression/v1's `check` is `remote mail suppression check`, remote/v1's `status` is `remote status`.
- **Flags:** one per field of the operation's input: `--at`, `--email`, `--campaign`.
  - Times take RFC 3339 (`2026-11-10T15:00:00Z`), a local time (`2026-11-10 15:00`) or a duration from now (`-2h`).
  - Lists take `a,b` or a repeated flag.
  - Anything else takes JSON, or `@file` to read it from a file.
- **Whole input:** `--json` takes the whole input as JSON (`@file` reads a file, `-` reads stdin). Flags you also
  give override its fields.
- **Which app:** `--remote` (`-r`) takes a remote's name or a URL. Without it you get the project's default remote.
- **Output:** JSON, so you can pipe it to `jq`. A stream (`remote logs`) prints one JSON line per entry until Ctrl-C.
- **Errors:** if the app doesn't offer the contract, the command says so ("this remote doesn't offer restore/v1").

In CI, set `P1_TOKEN` (or `P1_TOKEN_PROD` for one remote) to an [API token](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/tokens) instead of
signing in. [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes) covers remotes and saved logins.

## From a script: REST

Every operation is an endpoint under `/api/_c/<contract>/`:

```bash
curl -X POST https://myapp.example.com/api/_c/restore/v1/restore \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"at": "2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"}'
```

`GET /api/_c/remote/v1` is the one fixed path. It answers who you are and lists every contract the app offers.

## From an agent: MCP

An app serves MCP at `/mcp` ([MCP](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp)). Each operation is a tool named after its contract and
operation (`restore_points`, `restore_restore_to`, `remote_status`). Add `https://myapp.example.com/mcp` to Claude and
sign in.

## The same checks every way

The command, the endpoint and the tool all call the contract, so each passes the same checks:

- **Token scope:** each operation needs a token scope (`restore`, `restore:read`). An API token carries only the
  scopes it was given. A superuser's own sign-in passes all of them.
- **Superuser:** only superusers may call an operation, unless it's public.
- **Hooks:** the same hooks run, in Go and in `pb_hooks` (`onRestoreRestoreTo`).

## Every command, endpoint and tool

- [CLI reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli): every command of `pocketone`, PocketBase's own included.
- [REST reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/rest): every contract endpoint.
- [MCP reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/mcp): every contract tool.

Each [contract page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts) lists its operations all three ways. Each extension page lists the commands
it adds and the contracts it answers.

## Your own commands

An extension can replace a generated command with its own, or add new ones under `remote`, by providing
[cli.commands/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/cli.commands/v1). [Writing an extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension) explains how.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/agents

# Coding agents

PocketOne is new, so coding agents haven't seen much of it. Two things close that gap. Both are built from these docs, so they change when the docs change.

## Agent Skills

The `pocketone` plugin has three skills:

- **pocketone:** using PocketOne in an app: the `pocketone` binary and its commands, `pocketone.yaml`, deploying, and every extension.
- **pocketpages:** building PocketPages v1 sites in `pb_pages/`: routing, `ctx`, templates, layouts, auth and deploying.
- **pocketone-extensions:** writing your own extension and contributing it as a pull request: contracts, `extkit`, tests, and the README and changelog CI checks.

Each skill carries a copy of the docs in its `reference/` folder, so it works offline.

**Claude Code**

```
/plugin marketplace add pockethost/pocketone
/plugin install pocketone@pocketone
```

`/plugin marketplace update pocketone` picks up new versions.

**Other agents that read Agent Skills** (Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI and others)

```bash
npx skills add pockethost/pocketone
```

Or copy a skill folder into your project yourself. The skills live in [`agent/skills/`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/tree/main/agent/skills).

## llms.txt

For agents and tools that read the web:

- [pocketone.dev/llms.txt](https://pocketone.dev/llms.txt) indexes every docs page with a one-line summary.
- [pocketone.dev/llms-full.txt](https://pocketone.dev/llms-full.txt) holds every docs page in one Markdown file.

PocketPages' docs are part of this site, under [/docs/extensions/pages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages), so both files include them.

# Your hooks on QuickJS

PocketOne runs your `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations` on [QuickJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) instead of goja, the engine
stock PocketBase uses. It's the same JS API (`$app`, `routerAdd`, `onRecordCreate`, `cronAdd`, `$http`, …), so your
existing hooks run unchanged. On top of that you get:

- **Shared globals.** Top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler.
- **Imports.** ES modules with `import`/`export`, and `node_modules` packages.
- **TypeScript.** `.ts` hooks run directly.
- **Async.** Handlers can `await`, and the app keeps serving other requests while they wait.
- **Limits.** A runaway script stops with an error instead of taking the app down.

Each app gets one QuickJS VM. The engine is pure Go, so builds need no cgo, as with stock PocketBase.

This tutorial builds a small app that tries each of these. Every example below was run on `pocketone`, and the outputs
are real.

## Set up

Make a folder for the app, create a superuser, and start it:

```bash
mkdir -p qjs/pb_hooks/lib && cd qjs
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password --dir=pb_data
pocketone serve --dir=pb_data
```

Leave it running. PocketOne watches `pb_hooks`, so each file you add below is picked up without a restart.

## 1. Your PocketBase hooks run unchanged

Here's a hook written for stock PocketBase, with `require()` inside the handler and the global `$app`:

```js
// pb_hooks/legacy.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/legacy", (e) => {
  const util = require(`${__hooks}/lib/util.cjs`)
  return e.json(200, { shout: util.shout("hello"), users: $app.countRecords("users") })
})
```

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/util.cjs
module.exports = { shout: (s) => s.toUpperCase() + "!" }
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/legacy
# {"shout":"HELLO!","users":0}
```

A plain `.pb.js` file is still a CommonJS script, as in PocketBase. Nothing in it needs to change.

## 2. Top-level code is shared by every handler

On goja, each handler runs in a separate runtime from a pool, so it can't see the variables at the top of its own file.
That's why PocketBase hooks call `require()` inside every handler. On QuickJS, every hook file runs in the app's one
global scope:

```js
// pb_hooks/counter.pb.js
let hits = 0
function greet(name) {
  return `hi ${name}`
}

routerAdd("GET", "/hits", (e) => {
  hits++
  return e.json(200, { hits, msg: greet("there") })
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits   # {"hits":1,"msg":"hi there"}
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits   # {"hits":2,"msg":"hi there"}
```

The same file on goja (`pocketone serve --jsvm goja`) answers every request with a 400, because the handler can't see
`hits` or `greet`.

Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart or a change to `pb_hooks` starts a fresh one (`hits` goes back to 0),
so keep anything that must last in the database. Use globals for caches, helpers and constants.

Hook files run before the app opens its database, as in PocketBase. A `$app` query at a file's top level fails, so to
fill a global from the database, do it in `onBootstrap`:

```js
let users = null
onBootstrap((e) => {
  e.next() // the database is open after this
  users = e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users")
})
```

## 3. Split your code into modules

Name a hook file `.pb.mjs` and it's an ES module, with `import` and `export`:

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/slug.mjs
export const slugify = (s) =>
  s.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-|-$/g, "")
```

```js
// pb_hooks/modules.pb.mjs
import { slugify } from "./lib/slug.mjs"

routerAdd("GET", "/slug/{text}", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, { slug: slugify(e.request.pathValue("text")) })
})
```

```bash
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8090/slug/Hello%20World%21"
# {"slug":"hello-world"}
```

- `.mjs` files are ES modules; `.js` and `.cjs` files are CommonJS. Both kinds can load each other.
- `import` and `require()` find files the same way: relative paths first, then packages in `node_modules`.
- A module loads once per app, so every file that imports it shares the same instance and its state.

## 4. Write hooks in TypeScript

Name the file `.pb.ts` and write TypeScript:

```ts
// pb_hooks/typed.pb.ts
interface Total {
  count: number
  label: string
}

function total(count: number): Total {
  return { count, label: `${count} users` }
}

routerAdd("GET", "/typed", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, total(e.app.countRecords("users")))
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/typed
# {"count":0,"label":"0 users"}
```

PocketOne removes the types when it loads the file, with no build step. An error names the line in your `.ts` file.
Types aren't checked at run time: run `tsc --noEmit` or rely on your editor. The app writes the whole JS API's types to
`pb_data/types.d.ts`, and the [JSVM page](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm#types) has a `tsconfig.json` that uses it.

## 5. Async handlers

A handler can be `async`. Every Go function has an `.async` twin that does its work outside the VM and returns a
promise:

```js
// pb_hooks/async.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/slow", async (e) => {
  await sleep.async(2000) // waits outside the VM
  const n = await e.app.countRecords.async("users")
  return e.json(200, { waited: "2s", users: n })
})
```

Call `/slow`, and call `/hits` while it waits:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/slow &
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hits
```

`/hits` answered after 0.35 s, and `/slow` after 2.06 s. The app went on serving requests while `/slow` waited.

Without `.async`, a call that waits (`$http.send`, `sleep`) still lets other requests run, but those requests nest on
one stack and wait on each other: under load, a plain `sleep(100)` served 19 requests a second where
`await sleep.async(100)` served 481 ([How it performs](#how-it-performs)). Use `.async` for anything slow.

Two things to watch:
- After an `await`, other requests may have run in between. Use `e.app`, not the global `$app`.
- A transaction holds SQLite's write lock, so keep it short across `await`s.

### Why there's no VM pool

goja runs JS synchronously: while a handler waits on the database or an HTTP call, its runtime can't do anything else.
To serve requests at the same time, PocketBase keeps a pool of runtimes (15 by default, `--hooksPool`) and makes more
when they're all busy. Each runtime loads every hook file separately. That's why a handler can't see the top of its own
file, why state can't be shared between requests, and why memory grows with load.

QuickJS here works like a Node.js process. Each app has one VM with an event loop. While a handler waits, the loop runs
other requests, and the handler picks up again when its result arrives. There's one copy of your code and your
globals, so nothing needs a pool (`--hooksPool` is accepted and ignored).

As in Node.js, the JS itself runs one piece at a time. A handler that computes for a long time holds the loop until it
finishes or hits its time budget. Keep heavy work out of the request path, or move it into Go.

## 6. Memory and time limits

Each app has a memory cap, and each task has a time budget:

```js
// pb_hooks/limits.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/hog", (e) => {
  const junk = []
  while (true) junk.push("x".repeat(1024 * 1024))
})

routerAdd("GET", "/spin", (e) => {
  while (true) {}
})
```

Both requests fail and the app keeps running:

| Request | Stopped after | Error in the request log |
|---|---|---|
| `/hog` | 0.08 s | `InternalError: out of memory at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:3:36` |
| `/spin` | 5.0 s | `InternalError: interrupted at pb_hooks/limits.pb.js:5:27` |

Calls to `/hits` right after each one answered normally.

These are the limits in the `pocketone` binary:

| Limit | Default |
|---|---|
| Memory: the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds | 64 MiB per app |
| JS time per task | 5 s |
| Wall time per task, Go calls included | 30 s |

Change them in `pocketone.yaml` ([Configure with pocketone.yaml](https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml)):

```yaml
app:
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB # the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds
    task_time: 10s # JS time per task
    task_wall: 60s # wall time per task, Go calls included
```

With `task_time: 1s`, `/spin` stopped after 1.0 s instead of 5. A custom Go build sets the same limits in
`jsvm.Config.VM` ([JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm#configure)). On a multisite host each app has its own VM and its own
limits, so one app's runaway script doesn't stop the others.

## How it performs

The same hook file, on the `pocketone` binary with each engine (QuickJS, and `--jsvm goja` with its default pool of 15):

```js
// pb_hooks/bench.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/b/ping", (e) => e.json(200, { ok: true }))
routerAdd("GET", "/b/db", (e) => e.json(200, { n: e.app.findRecordsByFilter("_superusers", "id != ''", "", 10, 0).length }))
routerAdd("GET", "/b/cpu", (e) => {
  const items = []
  for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) items.push({ id: i, name: "item" + i, tags: ["a", "b", "c"] })
  return e.json(200, { n: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(items)).length })
})
routerAdd("GET", "/b/wait", (e) => { sleep(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) })
routerAdd("GET", "/b/waitasync", async (e) => { await sleep.async(100); return e.json(200, { ok: true }) })
```

Each route got 50 concurrent clients for 10 seconds (`hey -c 50 -z 10s`, after a 3-second warm-up), with
`--dev=false`, on an Apple M1 Max (10 cores):

| Route | QuickJS req/s | p50 | p99 | goja req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A JSON reply | 19,471 | 2.2 ms | 9.4 ms | 55,901 | 0.8 ms | 3.3 ms |
| A database query (10 rows) | 18,116 | 1.9 ms | 12.8 ms | 40,447 | 0.8 ms | 7.9 ms |
| CPU-heavy JS (2,000-object JSON round trip) | 84 | 591 ms | 648 ms | 409 | 91 ms | 525 ms |
| Waits 100 ms with `sleep(100)` | 19 | 1.93 s | 12.0 s | 491 | 102 ms | 113 ms |
| Waits 100 ms with `await sleep.async(100)` | 481 | 103 ms | 110 ms | – | – | – |

| Memory (resident) | QuickJS | goja |
|---|---|---|
| Idle, after start | 46 MB | 49 MB |
| After all the routes above | 313 MB | 3.1 GB |

What it shows:

- **goja does more requests a second.** Its pool runs handlers on every core at once. QuickJS runs an app's JS on one
  thread, like Node.js: about 18,000 short requests a second for one app, on one core.
- **QuickJS uses a tenth of the memory.** goja's runtimes each hold a copy of every hook file, and it makes more of them
  as load grows. On a host running many apps, that's the difference that counts.
- **Waiting costs nothing with `.async`.** `await sleep.async(100)` kept pace with goja's pool. A plain `sleep(100)`
  didn't, so use `.async` for anything slow.
- **CPU-heavy JS is slower.** Move heavy work into Go, a cron job, or a background task.

## Going back to goja

To run an app on PocketBase's own engine, set it in `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
app:
  jsvm: goja
```

You can also pass `--jsvm goja`. The startup lines list what that turns off: pages, `$mcp`, `$tokens`, `$bulkmail`, JS
contracts, shared globals and async handlers.

## Next

- [JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm): every file type, module resolution rule and setting.
- PocketBase's [JS docs](https://pocketbase.io/docs/js-overview/): the JS API itself, which is unchanged.
- [Coding agents](https://pocketone.dev/docs/agents): give your agent the PocketOne skill so it writes hooks the QuickJS way.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/pocketone-yaml

# Configure your app with pocketone.yaml

Every `pocketone` flag has a default. `pocketone.yaml` lets you change those defaults in one file, next to your app,
instead of typing them on every start. The same file holds each extension's options, and your secrets go in a `.env`
beside it.

Without the file, nothing changes: PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. Every step below was run on `pocketone`.

## 1. Write the file

In your app's folder, create `pocketone.yaml`:

```yaml
server:
  http: 127.0.0.1:8090
app:
  dir: ./pb_data
  dev: false
```

Check it, create a superuser, and start the app:

```bash
pocketone config check
# pocketone.yaml: ok (2 sections)
pocketone superuser upsert admin@example.com password
pocketone serve
```

`pocketone serve` listens on the address under `server`, and the data folder is `pb_data` next to the file. Relative
paths are relative to the file's folder, so the app starts the same from any working directory.

PocketOne looks for `pocketone.yaml` in the working directory, then next to the executable. `--config <path>` picks
another file.

## 2. Flags still win

A flag always beats the file. The file only changes the defaults:

```bash
pocketone serve --http=127.0.0.1:8091   # listens on 8091, whatever the file says
```

## 3. Keep secrets in a .env

Put secrets in a `.env` beside the file, and refer to them as `$VAR` or `${VAR}` in any value:

```bash
# .env
LISTEN=127.0.0.1:8090
STRIPE_KEY=sk_test_123
OTHER_SECRET=hidden
```

```yaml
server:
  http: ${LISTEN}
```

Your JS hooks don't see the `.env` unless you allow each name:

```yaml
app:
  env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY]
```

```js
// pb_hooks/env.pb.js
routerAdd("GET", "/env", (e) => {
  return e.json(200, { stripe: process.env.STRIPE_KEY || null, other: process.env.OTHER_SECRET || null })
})
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/env
# {"stripe":"sk_test_123","other":null}
```

`pocketone config check` says when it read secrets from a `.env`. Keep the `.env` out of git.

## 4. Set an extension's options

Each top-level key is a section owned by one extension. For example, keep three days of point-in-time history, and
give the app's JS more room:

```yaml
pitr:
  retention: 72h
app:
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB
    task_time: 10s
```

`js_limits` sets the limits of the JS engine your hooks run on; [Your hooks on QuickJS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs#6-memory-and-time-limits)
shows what they stop.

To see every section your binary knows, with each key, run:

```bash
pocketone config
```

The [pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference) lists the same, with each key's type, default and meaning.

## 5. Choose which extension does a job

Extensions offer their abilities through [contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together). When more than one
extension can do the same job, `providers` picks one. Both PITR and Backups can restore your data. PITR is used when
it's on, but you can choose Backups:

```yaml
providers:
  restore/v1: backups
```

The startup lines show the choice:

```
INFO standard: restore/v1 ← backups (providers:)
```

## The whole file

```yaml
server:
  http: ${LISTEN}
app:
  dir: ./pb_data
  dev: false
  env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY]
  js_limits:
    memory: 128MiB
    task_time: 10s
pitr:
  retention: 72h
providers:
  restore/v1: backups
```

## Next

- [pocketone.yaml reference](https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference): every section and key.
- [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config): how the file is found, `.env` rules, and loading it in your own Go build.


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension

# Create your own extension

A PocketOne extension is Go code compiled into your build. There are two kinds, by where they run:

- **App extensions** add to an app: Go routes, PocketBase hooks, collections, admin dashboard screens, a JS API for
  `pb_hooks`, contracts other extensions use. They run on every app: a standalone app, or each instance of a
  multisite host. Almost every extension is one.
- **Host extensions** add to a multisite host, the process that serves many instances: request gates (firewall, rate
  limits), TLS, middleware around every instance, instance sources, background jobs.

How a multisite host runs its instances (in-process with [pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker), in containers with
[docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker), or both) is the host's `runtime/v1` contract. App extensions don't depend on it.

## App extensions: `extkit`

Write an extension once, against [`extkit`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/extkit.go) (its own module,
`github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit`; core has no part in it), and the same value runs on every app:

```go
type Extension struct{ cfg Config }

func New(cfg Config) *Extension { return &Extension{cfg: cfg} }

func (p *Extension) Name() string { return "hello" } // config key, `_hello_` collections, logs

func (p *Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error {
    c := p.cfg
    if err := cfg.Decode(&c); err != nil { // this app's settings over the defaults (json tags)
        return err
    }
    app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se *core.ServeEvent) error { /* routes, UI extensions */ return se.Next() })
    return nil
}

// optional: a $hello global in the app's JS hooks
func (p *Extension) BindJS(app core.App, rt js.Runtime) { /* rt.Set("$hello", ...) */ }

// optional: its TypeScript declarations, added to each app's pb_data/types.d.ts
func (p *Extension) TypeScript() string { return `declare var $hello: { greet(name: string): string };` }
```

- **Every app has the [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard)** (tokens, mcp, pitr, deploy and the rest). Add yours
  to it: `set.Add(myextension.New(...))`. On a standalone app, build the app with `set.NewApp(...)`, or build it
  yourself and call `set.Register(app, jsvm.Config{...})`. The stock binary does the second: `pocketbase.NewWithConfig`,
  then `set.Register` ([`examples/pocketone`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/examples/pocketone/main.go)). Without the set:
  `extkit.MustRegister(app, extensions...)`, and `extkit.BindJS(app, vm, extensions...)` in jsvm's `OnInit`.
- **On a multisite host** every instance gets the set, with that instance's `extensions.<name>` settings over your
  constructor's defaults. `enabled: false` there means `Register` and `BindJS` are never called for that instance.
  What runs inside an instance depends on its runtime: pocker registers the set in-process; a docker instance runs
  the `pocketone` binary in its container, so it has the stock set (your own extras need your own image); an instance
  on a stock PocketBase image runs none, and gets only the contracts the host provides for it
  ([Working together](#working-together-contracts)).
- **Routes:** an extension has none of its own. Its API is contracts, mounted for you under `/api/_c/<id>/`; design
  the contract in `ext/contracts` first ([Working together](#working-together-contracts)). Admin settings go through
  `settings/v1` (`settingsv1.Add`). Only paths a standard fixes stay at the root (`/.well-known/*`, `/mcp`). The
  conformance test fails any other route unless `conformance.Options.AllowRoutes` lists it with a reason.
- **Process-wide settings** come from a `pocketone.yaml` section your extension owns (`extkit.NewSection`).
- **State per app:** keep it in `app.Store()`. Something shared across apps (a pool, a client) closes through
  `extkit.Closer`.
- **Name the command with `extkit.Command`:** when a message tells people what to run ("run 'pocketone login
  prod'"), build it from `extkit.Command` (default `pocketone`), never a literal. A build shipped under another name
  (PocketHost's, say) sets it once in `main`, or with `-ldflags "-X github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit.Command=pockethost"`.
- [bulkmail](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/bulkmail/extension.go) is the reference implementation, and
  [`ext/standard/example`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/standard/example/main.go) a complete program.

## Working together: contracts

> Start with [How PocketOne fits together](https://pocketone.dev/docs/how-pocketone-fits-together) for the idea: every API an extension offers is a named,
> versioned contract, any extension can provide one, and everything else (the dashboard, the CLI, agents, `pb_hooks`,
> other extensions) calls the contract, never the extension. This section is how to do it in code.

In short, when you design an extension:

1. **Find the contracts you need** in the [catalogue](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts). Use them; don't reach into another
   extension.
2. **Decide what you offer.** Anything a client calls is a contract. If one already promises it, provide that one
   (your extension then stands in for the current provider). If not, write the contract first, named for what it
   does, not for your extension.
3. **Declare it** in `Contracts()` and **provide it** in `Register`. The startup lines, whoami and the catalogue show
   it from then on.

Extensions never depend on each other by name. They depend on **contracts**: versioned Go interfaces in
[`ext/contracts`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts), such as `deploy/v1` or `mail.fallback/v1`. Every API an extension
offers is a contract too, served at `/api/_c/<id>/`: extensions have no routes of their own.

Every contract, standard or community, lives in `ext/contracts/<id path>/vN/` with a README like an extension's
(owners and a one-line summary in its front matter; `## Use`, `## Provide`, `## Extensions`, `## License`). Its
Extensions section is generated from every extension's `Contracts()`: who provides it, requires it and works with
it (`go run ./.github/extensions contracts`; CI fails when it's stale or when an extension names a contract that
doesn't exist). Whoever first creates a contract owns it, so an extension author who adds one owns both. Design the
contract first, then the extension that provides it.

An extension declares what it implements, requires and works with:

```go
func (e *Extension) Contracts() extkit.Contracts {
    return extkit.Contracts{
        Implements: extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"),
        Defaults:   extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"), // steps aside if another extension provides it
        WorksWith:  extkit.IDs("tokens/v1"), // used when present
    }
}

func (e *Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error {
    deployv1.Contract.ProvideDefault(app, myDeployer{})
    return nil
}
```

At startup PocketOne resolves every contract and prints who provides it:

```
standard: deploy/v1 ← fastdeploy (default deploy stepped aside)
standard: bulkmail off: needs mail.fallback/v1, which nothing provides
```

- **Look contracts up after registration** (in hooks, at serve time): `deployv1.Contract.Must(app)`. A lookup inside
  `Register` panics.
- **Defaults, conflicts, choices.** A default steps aside for any other provider. Two other providers of a contract that
  allows one fail the start until `pocketone.yaml` picks one (`providers: { mail.fallback/v1: mailrelay }`).
- **Wrappers** decorate whatever provides a contract (`Contract.Wrap`), in registration order.
- **Wire contracts** have an HTTP API at `/api/_c/<id>/<op>`, action hooks in Go (`deployv1.OnUpload`) and JS
  (`onDeployUpload`), an MCP tool per operation and a client. Every caller passes the same scope check and hooks.
- **From pb_hooks:** an app's JS declares and provides its contracts in `onContracts`, which runs once after
  `pb_hooks` load and before the seal (so before bootstrap):

  ```js
  onContracts((e) => {
    e.provide("mail.fallback/v1", { send(m) { /* ... */ } }) // a contract open to JS
    e.require("restore/v1")   // the start fails (dev mode: warns) when nothing provides it
    e.worksWith("tokens/v1")  // shown in the startup lines
    e.next()
  })
  ```

  The startup lines show it (`pb_hooks: provides mail.fallback/v1; requires restore/v1`). Methods run on pooled
  runtimes like any hook handler, so they can't use the file's local variables. A Go extension that *requires* a
  contract only JS provides is resolved before the JS runs: name `pb_hooks` under `providers:` for it in
  `pocketone.yaml`.
- **CLI:** every operation of a wire contract is a `pocketone remote ...` command with no code (`remote restore to
  --at -2h`), flags from its input. Provide [cli.commands/v1](../ext/contracts/cli/commands/v1/README.md) to replace
  one with your own, or to add one (`remote rehash`).
- **No imports between extensions.** An extension imports `extkit` and contract packages, never another extension's
  module (tests and examples may). What it needs from another goes in the contract package: tokens/v1 has
  `RegisterScope`, `FromRequest` and `WithScopes`; remote/v1 has its CLI client (`remoteclient`), which deploy's
  commands use.

## Compiled in, not loaded at run time

Extensions are Go packages linked into the binary, the way Caddy modules work. Go's `plugin` package (`.so` files)
isn't used:
- it needs identical toolchain and dependency versions;
- it can't unload;
- it rules out static `CGO_ENABLED=0` builds.

A build is a small `main.go`: the standard set with your extensions added, as a standalone app or a multisite host.

## Your module

PocketOne keeps PocketBase's module path, so upstream merges stay clean. Point it at PocketOne in your `go.mod`:

```
require ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase v0.41.1

replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase => github.com/pockethost/pocketone <commit or version>
```

Go only honors `replace` in the main module, so the final binary's `go.mod` needs this line, not only your
extension's.

## Admin screens: `UIExtensions`

The dashboard loads extensions before it starts its router:
- Each extension is a named file system served at `/_/extensions/<name>/`.
- Every extension's `main.js` is bundled into `/_/extensions.js`.

Add yours in the same `OnServe` hook:

```go
//go:embed ui
var uiFiles embed.FS

ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui")
se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui})
```

`ui/main.js` runs in the dashboard with its UI kit (`t.*`) and globals (`app.routes`, `app.store`, `app.pb`):

```js
// a new page, with a link in the header
app.routes.superuserOnly("#/hello", async () => {
    const res = await app.pb.send("/api/hello");
    return t.div({ className: "page" },
        t.div({ className: "page-content" }, t.h1({}, "Hello"), t.p({}, `Instance ${res.instance}`)),
    );
});
app.store.headerLinks.push({ href: "#/hello", icon: "ri-emotion-happy-line", label: "Hello" });

// add to an existing screen: screens marked with pbEvent fire mount:<name> with their element
document.addEventListener("mount:pageBackupsSettings", (e) => {
    e.detail.prepend(t.p({ className: "txt-hint" }, "Hello from an extension."));
});
```

- **More hooks:** `app.store.settingsNavGroups` adds entries to the Settings sidebar. Search `pbEvent:` in
  [`ui/src`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/tree/main/ui/src) for every screen you can add to (Backups exposes `pageBackupsSettings`, `backupsList`,
  `backupsSettingsForm`, `backupCreateModal` and `backupRestoreModal`).
- **No build step:** plain JS works. Bundle with Vite if you prefer.
- **Experimental upstream:** this UI extension API is undocumented and can change between PocketBase releases
  (`ui/README.md`). Keep `main.js` small, and test it after each upstream update.

## Host extensions

A multisite host is one process serving many instances. A host extension works on that process, for every instance.
Like app extensions, host extensions work together through contracts, on the host's own scope:

| Concern | Contract | Providers |
|---|---|---|
| What runs the instances (one or several, in preference order) | [runtime/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/runtime/v1) | [pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker), [docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker) |
| Which instances exist (the instance record) | [instance.source/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/instance.source/v1) | `instances.yaml` (default), [mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership) |
| Admit requests (firewall, rate limits) | [gate/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/gate/v1) | [firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) |
| TLS for the host's listener | [tls/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/tls/v1) | [autotls](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) |
| Middleware around everything | [http.wrap/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/http.wrap/v1) | [servertiming](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/servertiming) |

A host extension is a `multisite.Extension`: `Name()` and `RegisterHost(h)`, which provides its contracts on
`h.Scope` and provides nothing when it isn't configured (no section). Pass it in `multisite.Options.Extensions` (in
preference order), or `multisite.Link` it from an `init` so linking its package is enough. The host seals its scope
once, with `providers:` choices for host contracts, and logs who provides what:

```go
h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Choices: providers, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{
	servertiming.New(),         // http.wrap/v1, outermost
	autotls.New(),              // tls/v1 from the `autotls` section
	&pocker.Provider{},         // runtime/v1
	&docker.Provider{},         // runtime/v1 too, when there's a `docker` section
}})
```

```
multisite: runtime/v1 ← pocker, docker
multisite: tls/v1 ← autotls
```

Background work goes on `h.Background`, and an extension with `Close(ctx) error` is closed once every app has
stopped.

Some contracts are provided by the host for its instances (host-provided contracts), because the instance can't
answer them itself: docker runs stock PocketBase images, so the host answers remote/v1 for them. The host serves them
in `h.InstanceRoutes`, which run after the peer check, the blocked answer and the gates (firewall, rate limits) and
before the runtime, with the resolved instance in `multisite.InstanceOf(r)`:

```go
remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(h.Scope, myRemote)
h.InstanceRoutes = append(h.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return remotev1.W.HostHandler(h.Scope, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next)
})
``` Other servers in the fleet are [edge](../ext/edge) (`edge.EdgeSource`, the host's `Forward`), and
runtime-only hooks are pocker's `Starter`, `SetupApp`, `OnStart`, `OnEvent` and `Manager`
([POCKER.md](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker/pocker#extensions)).

App extensions that only need settings shared by every instance (mailrelay, s3-fallback, pitr) read their own
`pocketone.yaml` section on first use and stay app extensions: they work on any host and on a single app.

## Rules on a multisite host

On a multisite host, instances can belong to people who don't trust each other, and your Go code runs with the host's
full power, outside the JS sandbox:
- **Act only for the app you were called for.** Keep per-app state in `app.Store()`, and use `extkit.AppID(app)` for
  anything shared that must differ per instance (a bucket prefix, a rate-limit key); never build a path from request
  input.
- **Instance data needs instance auth.** Protect routes that read or change it with PocketBase's auth middlewares
  (`apis.RequireSuperuserAuth()`, record auth).
- **Exposing something to JS is a sandbox decision.** Expose a function to an instance's JS only if it's safe for a
  hostile tenant to call. See [How is this safe?](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox#how-is-this-safe).
- **Outbound calls follow the egress policy.** Go's default HTTP client already refuses private addresses. If your
  extension must reach a private service, give it its own `http.Client` and transport, and never let instance input pick
  the address.

## Contributing an extension

Extensions are welcome, from us and from you. Open a pull request that adds `ext/<your-extension>/`.

### Change PocketBase's core as little as possible

PocketOne stays close to upstream so every PocketBase release merges cleanly. If your extension needs something the
core doesn't offer yet:
- **Add the smallest hook that makes it possible:** an extension point or an override, not your extension's logic. A
  nil-checked function field, a list callers can append to, or an event, with upstream behavior unchanged when nothing
  is registered.
- **Make it generic.** Name it for what it allows ("storage backend for an app"), not for your extension. Assume someone
  else's extension will use it too, and that we'll offer it to upstream PocketBase.
- **Mark every changed line** in PocketBase's own files with `// PocketOne:` and a few words on why, so the next upstream
  merge knows what to keep.
- **Keep it separate:** the core change goes in its own commit, with a test, ahead of the extension.
- **Prefer what exists:** jsvm `OnInit`, `OnServe`, the record and request hooks, `BaseAppConfig.DBConnect`,
  `UIExtensions`. Many extensions need no core change at all.

### What an extension folder contains

```
ext/<name>/
  go.mod            module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/<name>
  README.md         the extension's docs, and its page on pocketone.dev (below)
  CHANGELOG.md      its changes, newest first (see Changelogs)
  TODO.md           optional: work that waits for something else to exist first (see Blocked work)
  <name>.go         the extension
  <name>_test.go
  conformance_test.go  the shared extension test (below)
  modes_test.go     the feature on the real binary, in every mode it runs in (below)
  example/main.go   a minimal program that builds cleanly and shows the feature
  ui/               optional: admin screens (embedded main.js)
  site/             optional: more end-user docs, as PocketPages pages (below)
  blog/             optional: posts for the pocketone.dev blog
```

- **`example/main.go` is required.** Keep it as small as possible: just enough to build a binary that shows the
  feature working, with no extra harness. `go build ./example` and `go vet ./...` must pass with no warnings.
  [`ext/standard/example`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/tree/main/ext/standard/example) and [`ext/sandbox/example`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/tree/main/ext/sandbox/example) are the size to aim for.
- **Examples come with two logins:** superuser `admin@example.com` and user `user@example.com` (verified, in
  `users`), both with password `password`. Every `example/main.go` calls
  `devusers.Register(app)` right after the app is created (on a multisite host, `devusers.Ensure(app)` in the
  host's per-instance setup), from [`ext/devusers`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/devusers/devusers.go). A fresh data dir is then ready to log
  in to, with no installer page and no CLI step. Never register it in a production build.
- **`conformance_test.go` is required.** It runs the shared extension test from
  [`ext/extkit/conformance`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/conformance/conformance.go) once:

  ```go
  func TestConformance(t *testing.T) {
  	conformance.Run(t, func() extkit.Extension { return myextension.New(myextension.Config{}) })
  }
  ```

  It checks that the extension registers, migrates, serves and shuts down on a fresh app with no goroutines left
  behind; that its only routes are contracts' (`/api/_c/<id>/`); that PocketBase's own collections are unchanged and every collection it adds is named `_<name>` or `_<name>_…`; and
  that one extension value serves several apps at once (as on a multisite host) without registering on one app
  touching another's hooks. An extension that requires another (`Contracts().Requires`) lists it in
  `conformance.Options{Deps: ...}`. An extension that adds MCP tools ([`ext/mcp`](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mcp#tools-from-an-extension)) also passes
  `conformance.Options{Setup: ...}` that registers MCP on the test apps; the test then checks each tool is named
  `<name>_<verb>_<noun>`, is described, and has an object input schema (`pb_` is reserved). Run it with `go test -race`. It's the minimum every extension passes; your own tests cover the
  feature.
- **`modes_test.go` tests the feature in every mode it runs in**, on the real `pocketone` binary, with
  [`ext/extkit/modetest`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/modetest/modetest.go). Declare the instances the test needs, each configured
  in full (files, extension settings, secrets), and the harness lays them out once per mode: `Single` (each its own
  `pocketone serve`), `Host` (one multisite host serving them all) and `Fleet` (several hosts that forward to each
  other). An app extension runs `modetest.AllApp` (Single and Host); a host extension picks Host and/or Fleet.

  ```go
  func TestModes(t *testing.T) {
  	top := modetest.Topology{Instances: []modetest.Inst{{ID: "app", Extensions: map[string]any{"myextension": map[string]any{"limit": 5}}}}}
  	modetest.Run(t, top, modetest.AllApp, func(t *testing.T, w *modetest.World) {
  		s := w.Instance("app")
  		s.MustJSON(http.MethodGet, "/api/_c/myextension/v1", s.Token(), nil, 200, nil)
  	})
  }
  ```

  The same test body runs in every mode: each instance has the URL `http://<id>.localhost:<port>` in all of them, and
  `World.Update`, `World.Add`, `World.Restart` and `Site.WaitRestarted` do what each mode does (a host reloads its
  instances file; a single app restarts its process). Where a mode really behaves differently, check `w.Mode` and say
  why in a comment. `-short` skips mode tests.
- **The README starts with front matter**: who owns the extension and its version (see [Ownership](#ownership)), and
  its entry in the [catalogue on pocketone.dev](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions): its `title`, its `group` (one
  of the ids in [`site/extensions.json`](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/site/extensions.json): `binary`, `many`, `services`, `saas`, `authors`) and
  a one-line `summary`. Nothing outside your folder lists your extension: the site finds it there.

  ```markdown
  ---
  owners: ["@your-github-handle"]
  version: 0.1.0
  title: "My Extension"
  group: services
  summary: "One line: what it does for someone running an app."
  ---
  ```

- **The README has five required sections**, in this order. It is also your extension's page on pocketone.dev.
  - `## Install`: how to get it (built into `pocketone`, or the lines to add to a Go build).
  - `## Configure`: the `pocketone.yaml` section, flags and settings screens. The site adds a table of your section's
    keys, generated from your `extkit.NewSection` defaults; describe each key with a `doc:"…"` struct tag.
  - `## Use`: day to day: the admin screens and what to click, the commands.
  - `## Integrations`: the extensions yours works with and how (multisite hosting goes here, not in the sections
    above), and how other extensions can build on yours (hooks, filesystem kinds, per-instance settings, Go
    and REST APIs).
  - `## Example`: the code that uses it. A sentence on what your `example/main.go` runs, then the whole file in a
    ```` ```go ```` block, exactly as it is; `go run ./.github/extensions examples` copies it in, and CI fails when the two
    differ. Without an example (an extension built into `pocketone`), say where to see it used.

  Write the first three for someone running one PocketOne app, not for a Go developer. Anything else (how it works,
  limits) goes in sections after these, and extra guides can sit next to the README as other `.md` files.
- **More docs than a README holds go in `site/`:** a folder of [PocketPages](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pages) pages that
  pocketone.dev serves under your extension's page, so `site/ctx/req.md` is `/docs/extensions/<name>/ctx/req`.
  [`ext/pages/site`](../ext/pages/site) (PocketPages' own docs) is the example.
  - `site/_private/toc.md` is its nav: `# Section` headings and `- [Title](page.md)` links. Your extension's pages
    show it as their sidebar, in place of the main docs nav (with a link back, your README page and your guides on
    top); the main nav lists your extension once, like any other.
  - Pages are templates: EJS runs in `.md` files as in any PocketPages app, so a code sample writes `<%%` for a
    literal `<%`. Partials go in `site/_private/`; the site's own (`browser`, for one) are found too.
  - Link the way GitHub does, relative to the file (`ctx/req.md`, `../routing.md`, `shot.png` beside the page); the
    site turns them into site URLs, and a link to a file that doesn't exist fails the build.
  - Content only: no `+` files (layouts, `+config.js`, middleware, API routes).
  - An `index.md` at the root of `site/` becomes your extension's landing page (`/docs/extensions/<name>`, where the
    catalogue links), and your README moves to `/docs/extensions/<name>/extension`. Without one, the README is the
    landing page. PocketPages' landing is a splash written with the site's `splash inset` and `announce` styles.
  - `blog/*.md` files are posts on the pocketone.dev blog at `/blog/<file name>`, with the same front matter as the
    blog's own (title, description, date, author, tags) and links relative to the file.
- **Extensions here are MIT.** The README ends with `## License` and the single line `MIT`. An extension under another
  license lives in its author's own repository, not here.
  [`ext/pitr/README.md`](../ext/pitr/README.md) is the example to follow.
- **Your pull request touches only your folder** (and, for a new contract, its folder in `ext/contracts`). Don't commit
  generated files: the site pages, nav, search index, `llms.txt` and contract indexes are rebuilt on `main` after your
  change merges ([`.github/regenerate.sh`](../.github/regenerate.sh)). To preview your page, run
  `cd site/sync && go run .` and don't commit what it writes outside your folder.
- **CI enforces all of this.** [`.github/workflows/extensions.yml`](../.github/workflows/extensions.yml) fails when an extension
  README is missing its owners, version, title, group or summary, one of the five sections or its MIT `## License`, or its Example doesn't match `example/main.go`, when it has no
  `CHANGELOG.md`, or when a module that implements `extkit.Extension` has no conformance
  test, then builds, vets and runs `go test -race` on every module the
  change affects: the modules it touches, every module that reaches one of them through a `replace`, or all of them
  for a core change. [`.github/workflows/site.yml`](../.github/workflows/site.yml) checks that the site builds from
  your README. Run everything CI runs on your pull request, locally, from the repository root:

  ```bash
  go run ./.github/extensions test            # what you changed since origin/main, committed or not
  go run ./.github/extensions test ext/<name> # or name the modules
  ```

  When it ends with `ok`, CI passes too.

  Tests that need an external tool (MinIO, Docker) skip themselves when it isn't installed, so they don't block CI.
- **Dependencies stay in your module.** Heavy libraries go in your extension's `go.mod`, never in core's.
- **Standalone first.** Where it makes sense, an extension works on one standalone app, and adds more on a multisite
  host.
- **MIT**, like PocketBase and the rest of this repo.

### Changelogs

Each extension keeps its changelog in its own folder, `ext/<name>/CHANGELOG.md`, so a change to it touches nothing
else. The root [CHANGELOG.md](../CHANGELOG.md) is for the rest: core, the `pocketone` binary, the site.

- **A user-visible change adds its line under `## Unreleased`** in the same commit, grouped under `### Upgrading`
  (steps for anything breaking), `### Added`, `### Changed` or `### Fixed`. One line per change, written for someone
  running an app, with the command, flag or config key.
- **Don't raise `version:` yourself.** Each PocketOne release raises the version of every extension with lines under
  its `## Unreleased`: minor when it has `### Upgrading` lines, otherwise patch. It renames that section to the new
  version and lists the extension in the release's notes, linked to its changes
  (`go run ./.github/extensions release vX.Y.Z`).

```markdown
# My Extension changelog

## Unreleased

### Added

- `myext.retries` in `pocketone.yaml`: how many times to retry a failed delivery (default 3).
```

### Blocked work

An extension may keep a `TODO.md` in its folder: the work on it that waits for something else to exist first (a
contract, another extension's change, a host feature). Each item says what it waits on, under a `**Waits on:**` line,
and what to do once that lands; delete the item when it's done. Work that isn't blocked doesn't go here: do it, or
leave it out. So a look across `ext/*/TODO.md` shows what each missing piece would unblock. The file isn't published:
pocketone.dev skips it.

### Ownership

Every extension and every contract has owners, listed in its README's front matter (GitHub handles); an extension
also has a version there. Whoever submits an extension or first creates a contract owns it, so an author who adds a
contract with their extension owns both.

Who approves an outside pull request:

| What it changes | Who approves |
|---|---|
| PocketBase's own code, the standard extensions, the site, docs, examples, CI | a maintainer |
| A community extension | one of its owners, or a maintainer |
| A contract | one of its owners, or a maintainer |
| A new extension or a new contract | a maintainer |

Owners are read from the base branch, never from the pull request, so a pull request can't make its author an owner
and approve itself. Nothing merges unless the checks pass. An extension's version goes up when PocketOne releases
with changes to it ([Changelogs](#changelogs)), and its Go module tag (`ext/<name>/vX.Y.Z`) follows that version. A
planned extension (a README and no code yet) stays at `0.0.0`.

```bash
go run ./.github/extensions approvers origin/main HEAD   # who may approve each area a change touches
```

## Planned extensions

Our own extensions live in this repo under [`ext/`](../ext), each as its own Go module (`github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/<name>`). See [ext/README.md](../ext/README.md).


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/reference/cli

# CLI reference

Every command of the `pocketone` binary with its [standard extensions](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard): PocketBase's own, the ones extensions add, and a `pocketone remote …` command for every operation of every contract, generated from it ([how](https://pocketone.dev/docs/remote)). `pocketone <command> --help` says the same.

## Global flags

Every command takes these.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--config` | string | – | the config file (default ./pocketone.yaml, else next to the executable) |
| `--env-file` | string | – | secrets for $VAR references in the config file (default .env beside it); never passed to the app |

## pocketone config

Lists the pocketone.yaml sections this binary understands, with their defaults

```
pocketone config
```

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | bool | – | print the sections as JSON (name, doc, owning extension, keys with types and defaults) |

From [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config).

### pocketone config check

Checks the config file: every section known and valid, every $VAR set

```
pocketone config check
```

From [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config).

## pocketone deploy

Deploys pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public and packages to a remote

```
pocketone deploy [remote]
```

Deploys the project's code set (pb\_\* folders except pb\_data, package.json, bun.lock(b), patches/, and the production node\_modules tree) to a remote. Only changed files are uploaded and the remote swaps them in. Hooks, pages and public files take effect by themselves; migrations and packages apply when the app restarts: pass --restart, or run 'pocketone restart' later.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--commit` | string | – | commit SHA to record (default: $GITHUB\_SHA, $CI\_COMMIT\_SHA, or git HEAD) |
| `--dry-run` | bool | – | list what would be deployed, deploy nothing |
| `-e`, `--exclude` | stringSlice | – | exclude patterns (pb\_data is always excluded) |
| `-i`, `--include` | stringSlice | – | add include patterns (default set: pb\_\*,pb\_\*/\*\*/\*,package.json,bun.lockb,bun.lock,patches,patches/\*\*/\*) |
| `-m`, `--message` | string | – | note to record with this deploy |
| `--no-node-modules` | bool | – | don't ship node\_modules; leave the remote's alone |
| `--node-modules` | bool | – | ship the production node\_modules tree (default with a package.json) |
| `--out` | string | – | write the deploy set to a local folder instead of deploying |
| `--restart` | bool | – | restart the app after deploying when migrations or packages changed |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | bool | – | list every file |

From [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy).

## pocketone dev

Keeps the project's code and a remote in step both ways (and streams the remote's logs)

```
pocketone dev [remote]
```

Syncs pb\_hooks, pb\_migrations, pb\_pages, pb\_public and the other pb\_\* folders, package.json, bun.lock(b) and patches/ both ways: edits here are uploaded half a second after you save, and changes on the remote (such as migrations the dashboard writes) are downloaded within seconds. node\_modules is only uploaded, when package.json or the lockfile changes. pb\_data is never synced. Hooks, pages and public files take effect by themselves; migrations and packages you upload apply when the app restarts: type r and Enter. State is kept in .pocketone/; files to leave out go in .pocketoneignore.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-e`, `--exclude` | stringSlice | – | exclude patterns (pb\_data is always excluded) |
| `-i`, `--include` | stringSlice | – | add include patterns (default set: pb\_\*,pb\_\*/\*\*/\*,package.json,bun.lockb,bun.lock,patches,patches/\*\*/\*) |
| `--no-logs` | bool | – | don't stream the remote's logs |
| `--no-node-modules` | bool | – | don't ship node\_modules; leave the remote's alone |
| `--node-modules` | bool | – | ship the production node\_modules tree (default with a package.json) |
| `--poll` | duration | `5s` | how often to check the remote for changes |
| `--prefer` | string | – | on the first sync, files that differ: local (upload yours) or remote (download theirs); default asks |
| `--push-only` | bool | – | only upload changes (the old one-way dev); never download |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | bool | – | list every file |

From [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy).

## pocketone docker

Release binaries for the docker runtime provider (docker.versions in pocketone.yaml)

From [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker).

### pocketone docker seed

Downloads the releases docker.versions lists that the cache doesn't have yet

```
pocketone docker seed
```

From [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker).

### pocketone docker update

Finds the latest patch of each docker.versions minor, records and downloads it

```
pocketone docker update
```

From [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker).

## pocketone link

Adds a remote (default name "default") and signs in to it

```
pocketone link <url> [token]
```

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--device` | bool | – | sign in on another device with a code (SSH, headless) |
| `--name` | string | `default` | remote name |
| `--no-browser` | bool | – | print the sign-in URL instead of opening a browser |
| `--token` | string | – | use this API token (pbt\_..., a PocketHost token, or a JWT) |
| `--token-stdin` | bool | – | read the token from stdin |

From [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes).

## pocketone login

Signs in to a remote and saves the login

```
pocketone login [remote]
```

Signs in to a remote: in the browser when the remote offers OAuth (--device for a code on another device), else with a pasted API token.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--device` | bool | – | sign in on another device with a code (SSH, headless) |
| `--no-browser` | bool | – | print the sign-in URL instead of opening a browser |
| `--token` | string | – | use this API token (pbt\_..., a PocketHost token, or a JWT) |
| `--token-stdin` | bool | – | read the token from stdin |

From [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes).

## pocketone logout

Forgets the saved login (and revokes it, for a browser login)

```
pocketone logout [remote]
```

From [Remotes](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/remotes).

## pocketone logs

Streams a remote's app logs

```
pocketone logs [remote]
```

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-n`, `--lines` | int | `100` | replay this many earlier lines (0..1000) |

From [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy).

## pocketone migrate

Executes app DB migration scripts

```
pocketone migrate
```

Supported arguments are:
- up            - runs all available migrations
- down [number] - reverts the last [number] applied migrations
- create name   - creates new blank migration template file
- collections   - creates new migration file with snapshot of the local collections configuration
- history-sync  - ensures that the \_migrations history table doesn't have references to deleted migration files


| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--dev` | bool | `true` | enable dev mode, aka. printing logs and sql statements to the console |
| `--dir` | string | `<the binary's folder>/pb_data` | the PocketBase data directory |
| `--encryptionEnv` | string | – | the env variable whose value of 32 characters will be used as encryption key for the app settings (default none) |
| `--hooksDir` | string | – | the directory with the JS app hooks |
| `--hooksPool` | int | `15` | only with `--jsvm` goja: the JS runtimes kept ready for hooks |
| `--jsvm` | string | `quickjs` | the JS engine: quickjs (PocketOne's) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility) |
| `--migrationsDir` | string | – | the directory with the user defined migrations |
| `--queryTimeout` | int | `30` | the default SELECT queries timeout in seconds |

From PocketBase.

| `--hooksDir` | string | – | the directory with the JS app hooks |

| `--jsvm` | string | `quickjs` | the JS engine: quickjs (PocketOne's) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility) |
| `--migrationsDir` | string | – | the directory with the user defined migrations |
| `--queryTimeout` | int | `30` | the default SELECT queries timeout in seconds |

### pocketone oauth clients

## pocketone pitr

Point-in-time restore of the database

From [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr).

Every `pocketone pitr` command takes these.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--dev` | bool | `true` | enable dev mode, aka. printing logs and sql statements to the console |
| `--dir` | string | `<the binary's folder>/pb_data` | the PocketBase data directory |
| `--encryptionEnv` | string | – | the env variable whose value of 32 characters will be used as encryption key for the app settings (default none) |
| `--hooksDir` | string | – | the directory with the JS app hooks |
| `--hooksPool` | int | `15` | only with `--jsvm` goja: the JS runtimes kept ready for hooks |
| `--jsvm` | string | `quickjs` | the JS engine: quickjs (PocketOne's) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility) |
| `--migrationsDir` | string | – | the directory with the user defined migrations |
| `--queryTimeout` | int | `30` | the default SELECT queries timeout in seconds |

### pocketone pitr restore

Restore the database as it was at --at, into --to, or in place on the next start

```
pocketone pitr restore
```

With --to, writes the database as it was at --at into that file (any time, also on a fresh machine with the same bucket config). Without --to, stages the restore in place; run it while the server is stopped: the swap happens on the next start.

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--at` | string | – | time to restore to (RFC 3339) |
| `--to` | string | – | write into this file instead of restoring in place |

From [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr).

### pocketone pitr status

Show the restorable window and history size

```
pocketone pitr status
```

From [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr).

```

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | bool | – | list what would be pulled |

## pocketone remote

The project's remotes, and the commands that run on them (every contract an app offers)

### pocketone remote add

Adds or replaces a remote

```
pocketone remote add <name> <url>
```

### pocketone remote restore points

Says what the app's data can be restored to: a window of time (continuous history) or a list of moments (backups), and whether a restore is running (restore/v1)

```
pocketone remote restore points
```

Says what the app's data can be restored to: a window of time (continuous history) or a list of moments (backups), and whether a restore is running.

Calls GET /api/\_c/restore/v1/ on the remote (token scope: restore:read).

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-r`, `--remote` | string | – | the remote (a name or URL); default: the project's default remote |

From [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) (generated).

### pocketone remote restore to

Puts the app's data back as it was at the given moment, from the latest point at or before it (restore/v1)

```
pocketone remote restore to
```

Puts the app's data back as it was at the given moment, from the latest point at or before it. The app restarts to apply it; its current data is kept aside until the next restore.

Calls POST /api/\_c/restore/v1/restore on the remote (token scope: restore).

| Flag | Type | Default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--at` | string | – | a time: RFC 3339 ("2026-11-10T15:00:00Z"), local ("2026-11-10 15:00"), or relative to now ("-2h") |
| `--json` | string | – | the whole input as JSON (@file reads a file, - reads stdin); flags override its fields |
| `-r`, `--remote` | string | – | the remote (a name or URL); default: the project's default remote |

From [restore/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/restore/v1) (generated).
